justice: Wide paved sidewalks on the right ensure equitable spatial distribution, easily accommodating pedestrians, strollers, and wheelchair users.
The absence of visible tactile paving (blind tracks) along the main walkway reduces fairness for visually impaired users.
Smooth paving surfaces and subtle curb transitions near the crosswalk enhance physical accessibility for older adults and people with disabilities.
safety: The physical planting strip separates the pedestrian/cyclist path from the roadway, heavily reducing conflict risks between motor vehicles and vulnerable groups like adolescents or the elderly.
Clear zebra crosswalk markings and roadside warning signs successfully alert drivers to potential pedestrian crossings.
The wide, straight vehicular lanes lack physical traffic calming measures (e.g., speed bumps), which may encourage speeding and pose a crossing risk for elderly pedestrians.
livability: The complete absence of street furniture like benches prevents older adults and disabled individuals from resting, significantly reducing the street's livability.
The adjacent water body and scenic view on the left provide a recreational aesthetic that enhances the daily quality of life for all residents.
The lack of visible active commercial frontages and low pedestrian presence reduce 'eyes on the street', limiting social surveillance and community vibrancy for teenagers and other users.
sustainability: The continuous planting strips with ground cover provide permeable surfaces that aid in urban rainwater infiltration.
The presence of a shared non-motorized pathway (indicated by the blue sign) actively supports low-carbon travel for both cyclists and pedestrians.
The newly planted street trees are currently immature, providing very limited ecological benefits such as carbon sequestration or microclimate regulation.
aesthetics: Fresh, uniform asphalt and distinct white lane markings create a highly clean and visually organized streetscape for all road users.
The consistent architectural style of the white buildings with dark roofs on the right adds cultural and visual coherence to the environment.
The scenic integration of the water body on the left with distant tree lines strongly enhances the visual appeal of the streetscape.
comfort: The sparse canopy of the newly planted trees offers minimal shade, leading to poor thermal comfort for older adults and pedestrians during hot weather.
The highly smooth, flat paving ensures excellent physical comfort and trip-free walking for the elderly and those using mobility aids.
The absolute lack of seating facilities negatively impacts physical comfort, as older adults or physically disabled users cannot rest during their journeys.
walkability: Continuous, wide sidewalks completely free of physical obstacles provide excellent walking conditions for all social groups.
Clearly marked crosswalks facilitate safe crossing points across the wide avenue, improving overall route connectivity.
The significant lack of shade trees and resting places drastically reduces the attractiveness and feasibility of long-distance walking for elderly and adolescent users.
bikeability: The blue circular sign on the right establishes a shared path, safely legitimizing cycling space away from motor vehicles for teenage and adult cyclists.
The green planting buffer separating the path from the road substantially increases cycling safety by protecting riders from fast-moving vehicles.
The lack of painted, dedicated bike lane dividers on the shared path may lead to right-of-way conflicts between fast cyclists and pedestrians.
